title: Illinois Lab Owner Rajesh Patel Charged in $66 Million Covid Testing Fraud
excerpt: A federal grand jury has indicted the Schaumburg co-owner on five wire fraud counts, alleging 380,000 fake negative PCR results were used to bill a federal programme for the uninsured.
body:
• A federal grand jury in the Northern District of Illinois has indicted Rajesh "Raj" Patel, 52, of Schaumburg, on five counts of wire fraud over an alleged $66.2 million Covid-19 testing scheme.
  • Prosecutors allege Patel created fake negative results for at least 380,000 PCR tests that his Hillside laboratory never performed between May 2021 and April 2022.
  • The lab submitted about $66.2 million in claims to the HRSA Uninsured Program and was paid about $44.1 million; Patel personally obtained about $28 million, the Justice Department says.
  • Reader takeaway: an indictment is an allegation and Patel is presumed innocent until proven guilty; if convicted, he faces up to 20 years in prison on each count.

A federal grand jury in Chicago has indicted an Illinois laboratory owner in a new Covid-19 fraud case, separate from the UK PPE sentencing covered earlier this week. Rajesh "Raj" Patel, 52, of Schaumburg, Illinois, is charged with five counts of wire fraud in connection with an alleged $66.2 million scheme to bill the government for Covid-19 tests that were never performed, the US Department of Justice announced. The indictment was returned in the Northern District of Illinois.

The case is materially distinct from the UK case involving Jogesh and Meenakshi Bhandari, who were sentenced in October over fake nitrile glove deals. Patel's case concerns PCR testing in Illinois, a different defendant, a different programme and a fresh indictment, not a sentencing.

"This defendant allegedly exploited a global crisis for personal gain, fabricating hundreds of thousands of COVID-19 tests – then billing the taxpayer for it."

— Colin M. McDonald, Assistant Attorney General, Justice Department Fraud Division

What Prosecutors Allege Happened

According to court documents cited by the Justice Department and reported by The Digital Free Press, Patel was co-owner and chief operating officer of a clinical laboratory in Hillside, Illinois, that processed PCR tests during the pandemic. Around March 2021, the laboratory entered an agreement with Meridian Medical Staffing Inc., which collected test specimens and patient information. The laboratory paid Meridian tens of millions of dollars.

https://x.com/Newsforce/status/2112759640014328262

Prosecutors say many of those patients never existed or never provided specimens to Meridian. Between May 2021 and April 2022, Patel allegedly created fake negative results for at least 380,000 PCR tests on specimens provided through Meridian, even though the laboratory never performed the tests. The fake results were then used to bill the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) Uninsured Program, the federally funded programme that covered Covid-19 testing costs for people without health insurance.

The Money and the Charges

The laboratory submitted approximately $66.2 million in fraudulent claims to HRSA and was paid approximately $44.1 million, according to the Justice Department. Patel personally obtained approximately $28 million in proceeds from the scheme, prosecutors allege. He is charged with five counts of wire fraud. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison on each count.

The case was investigated by the FBI Chicago Field Office and the US Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG). Trial Attorney Claire Sobczak Pacelli of the Fraud Division's Health Care Fraud Section is prosecuting. FBI and HHS-OIG officials said pandemic programmes were a lifeline for vulnerable people and that the scheme allegedly exploited a programme for the uninsured.

Separate UK Case: The Bhandari Sentencing

In the separate UK case, Jogesh Bhandari, 59, from Loughborough, was sentenced to eight years in prison at Leicester Crown Court on October 16 over fake PPE supply deals for nitrile gloves, according to reporting on the National Crime Agency investigation via Twasl News. His wife Meenakshi Bhandari received a two-year sentence suspended for two years with 250 hours of unpaid work, and associate Craig Morris, 43, was jailed for three years and nine months. The three were convicted after a five-week trial in July. Investigators said advance payments, including more than $3.18 million for gloves for US hospitals that never arrived and a $1.35 million payment, were spent on luxury cars, watches, jewellery, holidays and home renovations. The two cases share a pandemic-fraud theme but involve different people, countries and schemes, and no link between Patel and the Bhandaris is alleged in either announcement.

What's Next

Patel's case will proceed in federal court in the Northern District of Illinois. No trial date was given in the Justice Department announcement. The department notes that an indictment is merely an allegation and that all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
